title: A River That Brings Life
overview: Ezekiel sees a river flow out of the temple and bring the Dead Sea to life, then hears how the land will be shared out, including with foreigners.

parts.label: Water from the temple (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: In Ezekiel's vision of a restored temple, water seeps out from under the doorway and runs east, past the altar where sacrifices were offered. The temple was where God was believed to live among his people, so the picture is of life flowing out from God's presence into the land.

parts.label: The rising river (vv. 3-6)
parts.note: Every thousand cubits, roughly half a kilometer, the guide measures again and the water is deeper: ankles, knees, waist, then a river too deep to cross. No streams are said to join it, so many readers take the growth itself as the point: a gift that keeps increasing the further it goes.

parts.label: The Dead Sea made fresh (vv. 7-11)
parts.note: The river runs down the dry Jordan valley into the Dead Sea, so salty that almost nothing lives in it, and makes it fresh enough for fishermen to line its shores from one end to the other. The marshes stay salty, probably because salt was valuable for food, trade and the offerings at the temple.

parts.label: Trees of food and healing (v. 12)
parts.note: Trees on both banks bear fruit every month and their leaves heal, a picture of a land that never goes hungry or sick because its water comes from God's sanctuary. Christians later read this alongside the river and tree of life in Revelation 22, at the very end of the Bible.

parts.label: Borders of the land (vv. 13-20)
parts.note: The land is shared equally among twelve tribes, with Joseph counted twice through his two sons; Levi, the priestly tribe, gets no tribal share here but receives land within a holy area in the next chapter. The borders roughly match those given by Moses in the book of Numbers, though some of the places named can no longer be located with certainty.

parts.label: Room for foreigners (vv. 21-23)
parts.note: Foreigners who have settled and raised families are to receive land just like those born Israelite, in whichever tribe they live. Earlier laws protected foreigners but did not give them a permanent family share, so this is a striking widening of who belongs.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether this vision describes a real future temple, river and land division in Israel, or is a symbolic picture of God's life spreading out into the world.
think: Ezekiel imagines the most lifeless place he knew becoming full of life; is there anything in your own world you have written off as beyond changing?
